results.summary: This design is a test module that either outputs a counter to its 8 outputs and bidirectional pins or mirrors its 8 inputs to the outputs, depending on the state of input 0. It is used by setting input 0 high and observing that the outputs toggle. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself. This is a simple factory test pattern with minimal documentation.

This design generates a 5-pin VGA signal from a 25 MHz clock, displaying a clock with three bars whose heights represent hours, minutes, and seconds. It is tested on an FPGA and requires a VGA screen connected to the pins. The Verilog is generated from a SpinalHDL project and manually adapted to the TT03p5 requirements. The design uses only one digital pin per color channel, limiting color depth.

This circuit drives a 16x16 P10 LED panel, initially displaying the string 'TT03P5'. It accepts a 1.2 Mbaud UART input to paint pixels, erase pixels, clear the display, and change the displayed color, but resource limitations restrict it to a single color at a time and no double buffering. A mode pin allows selection between two clocking patterns to accommodate different panel wiring. External hardware includes an LED panel and a level converter to 5V logic.

This design implements a 128-byte DFFRAM module with address, write enable, and data input/output pins. The documentation consists only of 'TODO' placeholders, so the exact functionality and usage are not described. The pin names indicate a memory interface with 7 address bits, a write enable, 8 data inputs, and 8 data outputs. No test or usage information is provided.

This design implements the 'Simon Says' memory game, where the user repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors, each associated with a tone played on a speaker. It requires four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, and optionally a speaker or buzzer; the game is reset and then started by pressing any button. The design needs a 50 kHz clock input and has been tested in the Wokwi online simulator. It is a simple educational game with clear documentation.

This design is a proof-of-concept SRAM controller for 128 bytes of memory, with pins for address, write enable, and data input/output, including a bank select signal that multiplexes some bidirectional pins. The documentation is entirely 'TODO', so the detailed operation and usage are not described. The pin names suggest a banked memory interface with 9 address bits and 8 data bits. No test or implementation details are provided.

This design shows the time on a VGA screen using a 31.5 MHz clock, with pins for hsync, vsync, and 6-bit color output (two bits per RGB channel). It uses a pre-generated font loaded into registers and 'races the beam' to generate the display. External hardware includes an R2R DAC to convert the digital color outputs to analog VGA signals and a VGA monitor. The design supports adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds via input pins.

This Wokwi project outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display, using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through the characters. The counter increments with a 1 Hz clock and resets after 11, determining which character is displayed. Test inputs include a reset counter, clock disable, and four test logic pins, but the testing procedure is not explained in the documentation. The truth table for the design is provided in an external spreadsheet.

This design is an asynchronous ternary selector, with pins named for ternary inputs and outputs, including error flags and test controls. The documentation is minimal, with only placeholder text for how it works and how to test. The pin names suggest a ternary logic function, but the exact operation and usage are not described. It is likely a process or logic experiment.

This design, named LFMPDM (Lightning Fast Matrix Programmable Design Module), implements 8 four-input look-up tables (LUTs) that can be configured via input pins. The documentation contains only placeholder text for how it works and how to test, so the detailed operation is not described. The pin names indicate an address/data bus for loading configuration, a data input, and a single output. It appears to be a small programmable logic block but lacks sufficient documentation.
